channel.title: Witness Camera
channel.description: Guides on filming police and ICE, the law around recording, and how Witness Camera works. An independent iOS app for documenting encounters with law enforcement.

item.title: Stealth mode camera app for iPhone and Android: what it can hide
item.description: What a stealth or black-screen camera app can and cannot hide on iPhone and Android, why the recording indicator stays, and the legal question that matters first.

item.title: How to hash video footage and prove it has not been altered
item.description: What a SHA-256 hash of a video proves, how to compute and compare one on any computer, and how Witness hashes every piece of footage on the phone before upload.

item.title: Trusted timestamp for video: how RFC 3161 time-stamping works
item.description: How an independent time-stamp authority proves a video existed at a given time, how to verify a .tsr token with OpenSSL, and what Witness sends to the authority.

item.title: Chain of custody for video: what a manifest records and how to check it
item.description: What a video chain-of-custody log should contain, what Witness writes in its session manifest (hashes, UTC times, location, authority), and how to verify it.

item.title: Record video straight to the cloud while you are still recording
item.description: Why ordinary cloud backup only uploads after you stop, and how Witness uploads a piece every 15 seconds to Google Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud or WebDAV as you record.

item.title: Send video and your location to a trusted contact while you record
item.description: How Witness shares each recording with an emergency contact as it arrives and lets you send your last known location with one tap. Free.

item.title: Burn a timestamp and GPS location into video on iPhone and Android
item.description: How to put the date, time and coordinates on screen in your video with Witness Pro, how it differs from the hidden hash and manifest, and when outlets want it.

item.title: Start recording video without unlocking your phone
item.description: How to start a recording in one press from the iPhone Action Button, Lock Screen widget or Siri, or an Android Quick Settings tile, widget or assistant shortcut.

item.title: Record video straight to Nextcloud or your own WebDAV server
item.description: How to send video to your own Nextcloud or WebDAV server while recording, why it keeps footage away from US cloud providers, and the trade-off on sharing.

item.title: Trim silence out of video automatically: the highlight cut
item.description: How Witness Pro automatically makes a shorter cut of a recording with the quiet dead air removed and the speech kept, and how it decides what counts as speech.

item.title: Record with the front and rear camera at once on iPhone and Android
item.description: How dual-camera recording works in Witness: front and rear together, the 1080p limit, how Pro settings turn it off, and device support.

item.title: Record video on a weak connection: how Witness sends a preview first
item.description: What happens to uploads on a crowded or slow mobile network: queueing, retries, nothing deleted until confirmed, and a low-resolution stand-in copy sent first.

item.title: Does Witness encrypt video? What protects footage and what does not
item.description: An honest answer: Witness adds no encryption layer of its own. What protects footage on the phone and in your cloud, what does not, and which tools to look at.

item.title: Generate a PDF evidence report from a video recording
item.description: What a Witness evidence package contains: a PDF report with timeline, device, location and segment hashes, the manifest and time-stamp proof, with no video.

item.title: How to blur faces and anonymise voices in protest video
item.description: A practical workflow for protecting people in footage: keep the original, blur a copy, treat pitch shifting as weak, and use subtitles. Tools, limits and risks.

item.title: Witness for journalists: footage that survives a seized phone
item.description: How journalists use Witness to keep footage safe, show where it came from and deliver it to an editor. Free on iPhone and Android, with optional Pro.

item.title: For newsrooms: verify footage recorded with Witness in ten minutes
item.description: A step-by-step check for verification desks: what to ask a contributor for, the hash and time-stamp commands, what a pass proves, and what it does not.

item.title: Witness for documentary and investigative filmmakers
item.description: Shooting quality with provenance: 4K, Apple Log or HDR, ProRes, dual camera and evidence packages, with the upload and file-size trade-offs stated plainly.

item.title: For lawyers: what a Witness evidence package contains and proves
item.description: What lawyers receive from Witness footage: manifest, hashes, independent time-stamp and a PDF report, what they establish, and what they do not.

item.title: Witness for legal observers and legal-support teams
item.description: How legal observers can use Witness at demonstrations: shared storage, a coordinator as emergency contact, footage that survives a seized phone, and limits.

item.title: Witness for NGOs and human rights teams: a field workflow
item.description: A documentation workflow for civil-society teams: where footage goes, device policy, training, evidence packages, and how Witness compares with Tella.

item.title: Tamper-evident documentation for work sites, tenancies and claims
item.description: Using Witness to document site conditions, tenancies and damage claims with hashed, time-stamped video, and when a dedicated inspection tool is better.

item.title: Is Witness Pro worth it? Who should pay, and who should not
item.description: An honest buyer's guide to Witness Pro: what it adds, what free camera apps already do, the monthly versus one-time price, and who should skip it.

item.title: How to film a dispersal order at a protest: what to capture
item.description: When police order a crowd to disperse: what to film (who gave the order, whether it was audible, the way out, the time) and why to leave. Free app.

item.title: Filming an arrest at a protest: distance, identification, minors
item.description: How to film an arrest at a protest without getting in the way: what to capture, what not to do, and what to do with footage of a minor. Free app.

item.title: Student and campus journalists: filming protests safely and lawfully
item.description: Campus reporters filming protests: legal exceptions that may or may not apply, verifying footage, protecting minors and sources, and a safe workflow.

item.title: After the protest: who to give footage of police conduct to
item.description: What to do with footage of police conduct at a protest: keep the original, take advice, and the official routes in France, Greece, Spain, Germany and Italy.

item.title: Protest phone checklist: 10 steps before you film the police
item.description: Ten steps to prepare your phone before a protest: passcode, battery, cloud storage, test recording, emergency contact and exits.

item.title: Police ask you to delete your protest video or take your phone: Europe
item.description: What to do if an officer tells you to stop filming, delete a video or hand over your phone at a protest in Europe, and what the law says in five countries.

item.title: If your teenager goes to a protest: how to prepare their phone
item.description: A parent's guide to preparing a teenager's phone for a school or student protest.

item.title: Filming the police at student protests across Europe
item.description: Student and school protests in France, Italy, Germany, Greece, Spain and Portugal: what is happening, what stays the same everywhere, and where to find the guide for your country.

item.title: Witness for Professionals: how Witness Pro works
item.description: What Witness Pro adds for journalists, documentary makers and investigators, what stays free, and the file-size and upload-speed trade-offs of 4K, ProRes and HDR.

item.title: ICEBlock was removed: what you can still use to document ICE
item.description: ICEBlock and similar sighting apps were pulled from the App Store and Google Play. What happened, how reporting apps differ from documenting apps, and what is still available.

item.title: Witness Record is now Witness Camera: what changed, what didn't
item.description: The app formerly called Witness Record is now Witness Camera, same developer, same design, only the name changed. What it is, who builds it, and how it differs from the other apps and organisations called Witness.

item.title: Witness App: which one do you actually mean?
item.description: Witness App could mean at least nine different things: a police-recording app, a human rights charity, a citizen journalism map, a puzzle game, and more. Find the one you want.

item.title: Apps for recording police, compared honestly by one of the developers
item.description: Cop Watch, TurnSignl, Legal Equalizer, the stock camera and Witness, compared on when footage actually leaves the phone. Written by the developer of one of them.

item.title: Filming the police in Europe: the law is different in every country
item.description: Unlike the US, there is no single European right to film the police. What is shared across the continent, what differs by country, and detailed guides for ten European and Latin American countries.

item.title: Who made Witness Camera? The developer, and what he can and cannot see
item.description: Witness Camera is built by Olmo Parenti, an independent solo developer. Who he is, why the app has no server, exactly what he can and cannot access, and the conflicts he declares.

item.title: How to film the police: step by step, as a bystander or when you are the one stopped
item.description: A step-by-step method for filming police in the US, including the case most guides skip: what to do when you are the person being stopped, pulled over, or detained rather than a bystander.

item.title: How to record police safely: distance, what to film, what to say
item.description: Practical guidance on filming law enforcement without making things worse: where to stand, what to actually capture, how to narrate, and the phone setting to change before you need it.

item.title: How to film at a protest: positioning, kettles, mass arrests and what not to post
item.description: Filming police at a demonstration is a different job from filming a single encounter. Where to stand, how to read a crowd, what to capture during a dispersal or mass arrest, and the ethics of posting crowd footage.

item.title: Can police take your phone or delete your video? Seizure, search and what to say
item.description: Whether officers can take your phone, search it, or delete footage, what Riley v. California actually decided, why seizure and search are different questions, and what to say if it happens.

item.title: Is it legal to record police? Can they take your phone? Answers
item.description: What the federal circuits have actually held about filming police, whether officers can seize or search your phone, buffer-zone laws, audio consent, and whether the footage holds up.

item.title: How to film ICE: what to capture at a street stop, a workplace, a courthouse or a home
item.description: Filming immigration enforcement changes with where it happens. What to capture at a vehicle stop, a workplace raid, a courthouse, a school or hospital, and an apartment building, plus what to do with the footage afterwards.

item.title: How to film ICE safely: warrants, agent ID, and keeping the footage
item.description: Recognising unmarked vehicles and plain-clothes agents, telling a judicial warrant from an I-200, what to film, blurring faces before posting, and making footage survive.

item.title: ICE at your door: what to film, what to say, and the warrant question
item.description: What to record when immigration agents are at your home: telling a judicial warrant from an I-200, why the door stays closed, what to say through it, and how to make sure the footage survives.

item.title: How to record on iPhone with your screen off: four methods, and the settings that stop it failing
item.description: Step-by-step methods for recording video on an iPhone with a dark screen, the Settings changes that stop the recording ending early, how to start without unlocking, and what to do when it stops on its own.

item.title: How to record video with the screen off on iPhone, and what iOS will not allow
item.description: What a black screen actually means on iOS, why the camera indicator cannot be hidden, when discreet recording is lawful, and how to record with the display dark.

item.title: Best iPhone apps for filmmakers and journalists, with the conflicts disclosed
item.description: Camera, audio, verification, editing and security apps worth having on an iPhone for film and reporting work, what each is actually for, and where the free option is genuinely the right one.

item.title: The ACLU Mobile Justice app shut down. What to use instead.
item.description: Mobile Justice was discontinued in February 2025 after running in 17 states and DC. What it actually did, what you lose without it, and how to choose a replacement.

item.title: How to keep police footage safe: chunked upload, hashing, timestamps
item.description: Footage leaves the phone in 15-second pieces while you film, each SHA-256 hashed and counter-signed by an RFC 3161 time-stamp authority.

item.title: Setting up Witness before you need it: storage, triggers, practice
item.description: Connecting storage, binding the Action Button, naming an emergency contact and practising the stop gesture, plus what to do if the phone is taken.

item.title: How to verify video evidence has not been altered | Witness
item.description: Confirm a recording is unedited and predates a given moment, using OpenSSL on your own machine. Written for lawyers, newsrooms and courts.

item.title: Recording police: storage, privacy and evidence questions | Witness
item.description: Can the developer see your footage, what happens if your phone is seized, which cloud services work, and whether the recording holds up as evidence.
